newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed seeks Chernomyrdin talks, no meeting planned.
newsitem.headline: Lebed seeks Chernomyrdin talks, no meeting planned.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed wants to brief Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Wednesday on his talks with Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, Russian news agencies said.
But sources close to the prime minister told the agencies that Chernomyrdin had planned no meeting with Lebed, President Boris Yeltsin's envoy to Chechnya, and had a full schedule.

The prime minister, who is handling some duties for Yeltsin, who is in hospital awaiting a heart operation, was due in St Petersburg late in the afternoon for talks with the organisers of the city's bid to stage the 2004 Olympic Games.

It was not clear if Lebed, who returned to Moscow early on Wednesday, would seek to talk to Chernomyrdin by telephone. Lebed has tried and failed to arrange meetings with Yeltsin on his return from previous trips.

The agencies quoted Lebed as saying Tuesday's talks had been "highly successful". Lebed pledged Moscow would press ahead with a planned troop withdrawal from Chechnya which was suspended by army commanders last week.
"Even by the end of the week, Viktor Chernomyrdin will get personally involved in the negotiating process," Interfax quoted Lebed as saying.
But Tass quoted sources close to Chernomyrdin as saying a meeting between him and Yandarbiyev was "scarcely possible".
Lebed, a former paratroop general, had harsh words for the Russian commanders in the region, whom he met on Tuesday before his talks with the separatists.
Tass said Lebed was "fed up with the situation in which the command makes announcements like that on the suspension of the troop withdrawal".
But Lebed said he had reached agreement with army commander General Vyacheslav Tikhomirov. "I hope we will have no more of such falling out of step," he said.
Lebed said Yandarbiyev had agreed Russian law should operate across Chechnya. There was no confirmation from the separatists, who have introduced Islamic sharia law in the region.

Both sides confirmed their commitment to last month's peace deal. Lebed said they would push ahead with the demilitarisation of the Chechen capital Grozny and had agreed in principle on forming a coalition government -- a potential sticking point.
A meeting to discuss the formation of the new government last week was boycotted by Chechnya's pro-Moscow leader, Doku Zavgayev, who says it is too early to talk about a coalition.
Interfax quoted the army saying there were three shooting incidents in Chechnya overnight. No soldiers were injured.
An army spokesman later told the agency dozens of armed supporters of pro-Moscow Chechen leader Doku Zavgayev may be planning to stage a raid in Grozny.
The report could not be confirmed. Rumours of such a move have been denied by Zavgayev and previously dismissed by Russian and separatist forces jointly patrolling the city.

Zavgayev, elected with Moscow's backing in a December 1995 vote riddled with irregularities, has been in Moscow since rebels seized much of Grozny on August 6. He boycotted a meeting last week aimed at starting moves to form a coalition government.
